walkthroughs.body_html:
Component 3: Poetry (Named Poet and Specified Movement) — a core area of A-Level English Literature.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Component 3: Poetry (Named Poet and Specified Movement) brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Component 3: Poetry (Named Poet and Specified Movement).

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What did Romantic poets value in nature?
options: Romantic poets believed nature was full of fairies and elves.
Romantic poets just liked to write about pretty landscapes.
Nature as a source of spiritual insight and emotional truth, accessed through imagination — not picturesque scenery for its own sake.
Context is required because all texts are about history.

mcqs.q: Why does historical context matter when reading literature?
options: Context is required because all texts are about history.
Texts emerge from and respond to specific historical conditions — context illuminates references, assumptions and arguments that might otherwise be invisible.
Context just means writing about what the author had for breakfast.
The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.

mcqs.q: Why distinguish the speaker of a poem from the poet?
options: Romantic poets believed nature was full of fairies and elves.
The speaker is the voice constructed in the poem; the poet is the writer. Treating them as identical can mislead, especially with dramatic monologues or personae.
The speaker of a poem is always the poet themselves.
The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
